items.stem: What is the main purpose of an explanation text?
options: To explain how or why something happens
To persuade the reader to buy something
To entertain with a made-up story
items.answer: To explain how or why something happens
items.markingKey: Explanation texts describe processes and causes (how/why).

items.stem: This sentence uses a technical vocabulary: ‘It is connected to the back of the throat by a narrow passage known as the Eustachian tube.’ Explain how this feature helps the reader.
items.answer: Technical vocabulary: ‘Eustachian tube’ is the precise scientific name.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for identifying technical vocabulary; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: ‘Eustachian tube’ is the precise scientific name.

items.stem: This sentence uses a causal connective: ‘Because the cover slopes, these droplets run down into a collecting channel’ Explain how this feature helps the reader.
items.answer: Causal connective: ‘Because’ explains why the droplets move.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for identifying causal connective; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: ‘Because’ explains why the droplets move.

items.stem: Identify one feature of explanation writing in this sentence and explain its purpose: ‘Because the cover slopes, these droplets run down into a collecting channel’
items.answer: Causal connective: ‘Because’ explains why the droplets move.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for the feature (causal connective); 1 for the example; remaining mark(s) for its purpose for the reader.

items.stem: Identify one feature of explanation writing in this sentence and explain its purpose: ‘Have you ever noticed your ears “pop” as a plane comes in to land?’
items.answer: Question to engage the reader: it links the topic to the reader’s own experience.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for the feature (question to engage the reader); 1 for the example; remaining mark(s) for its purpose for the reader.

items.stem: Read an explanation text, ‘Why Do Your Ears Pop?’. ‘Have you ever noticed your ears “pop” as a plane comes in to land? The cause is a difference in air pressure. Behind each eardrum is a small air-filled space called the middle ear. It is connected to the back of the throat by a narrow passage known as the Eustachian tube. Normally, the air pressure on both sides of the eardrum is the same. However, when a plane descends, the air pressure in the cabin rises quickly. The higher pressure outside pushes the eardrum inwards, which can feel uncomfortable or even painful. Swallowing or yawning opens the Eustachian tube briefly, allowing air to flow into the middle ear until the pressures are equal again. The “pop” you hear is the eardrum springing back into place.’ How does the writer explain why ears pop in a way that suits a general reader?
items.answer: Opening question linking to experience; technical terms explained (middle ear, Eustachian tube); clear cause-effect chain with ‘However’; practical tip (swallowing or yawning); final sentence explains the pop.
items.markingKey: Level-marked: top band (3–4) perceptive analysis with precise references; middle (2) clear explanation of some effects; lower (1) mainly retelling. [4]

items.stem: Read this from an explanation text, ‘How a Monsoon Forms’: ‘the land in South Asia heats up much faster than the surrounding ocean’ What happens to the land in summer?
options: It heats up faster than the ocean
It cools faster than the ocean
It stays the same temperature as the ocean
items.answer: It heats up faster than the ocean
items.markingKey: Retrieval: the answer is stated in the quotation (‘the land in South Asia heats up much faster than the surrounding ocean’).

items.stem: Explain the difference between skimming and scanning, and give one situation in which you would use each.
items.answer: Skimming is reading quickly for the gist (e.g. deciding whether an article is useful); scanning is searching for a particular detail (e.g. finding a train time in a timetable).
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: skimming defined; scanning defined; credit for apt situations.

items.stem: Explain how subheadings and topic sentences help a reader to skim a text.
items.answer: They summarise what each section is about, so the reader can grasp the main ideas quickly without reading every word.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: summarise sections; speed/finding the gist.

items.stem: Read this part of an explanation text, ‘How a Monsoon Forms’: ‘This sea air carries enormous quantities of water vapour. When it meets mountains such as the Western Ghats or the Himalayas, it is forced upwards, cools and condenses into thick clouds. As a result, heavy rain falls, sometimes for weeks at a time.’ Give two reasons why heavy rain falls when moist air meets mountains. Use your own words where possible.
items.answer: The air is forced upwards; it cools and condenses into clouds.
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark per valid point, up to 2: air forced upwards; air cools; vapour condenses into clouds. Do not credit copied irrelevant detail.

items.stem: Read this part of an information text, ‘The Waggle Dance’: ‘The direction of the straight run shows the direction of the food in relation to the sun. The length of the waggle tells the other bees how far away it is: the longer the waggle, the further the flight.’ Identify the two pieces of information the waggle dance gives to other bees. Use your own words where possible.
items.answer: The direction of the food relative to the sun and how far away the food is.
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark per valid point, up to 3: direction (relative to sun); distance (length of waggle). Do not credit copied irrelevant detail.

items.stem: Read this part of an explanation text, ‘Why Do Your Ears Pop?’: ‘Swallowing or yawning opens the Eustachian tube briefly, allowing air to flow into the middle ear until the pressures are equal again. The “pop” you hear is the eardrum springing back into place.’ Give two ways of making your ears pop, and explain why they work. Use your own words where possible.
items.answer: Swallowing or yawning: both open the Eustachian tube so air flows into the middle ear and the pressures equalise.
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark per valid point, up to 4: swallowing; yawning; opens tube / equalises pressure. Do not credit copied irrelevant detail.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. ‘Octopuses are among the most intelligent invertebrates. They can solve puzzles, open jars to reach food and even escape from aquarium tanks. An octopus has about 500 million nerve cells, and around two-thirds of them are in its arms rather than its brain, so each arm can explore and react partly on its own. Octopuses can also change the colour and texture of their skin in a fraction of a second to hide from predators.’ (a) Skim the paragraph ‘Clever Octopuses’ and state its main topic in a few words. (b) Give three pieces of evidence that octopuses are intelligent or unusual.
items.answer: (a) Clever Octopuses (b) They solve puzzles and open jars; they escape from tanks; most of their nerve cells are in their arms; they change colour and texture to hide.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: main topic identified [1] (b) Award 1 mark per valid point, up to 3: solve puzzles/open jars; escape tanks; nerve cells in arms; change colour/texture. [3]

items.stem: Read the paragraph. ‘Cities are often several degrees warmer than the countryside around them, an effect known as the urban heat island. Dark roads and roofs absorb sunlight during the day and release the heat slowly at night. Cars, air conditioners and factories add extra heat. There are also fewer trees and plants to provide shade and cool the air. Planting trees and painting roofs white are two ways to reduce the effect.’ (a) Scan an explanation text, ‘How a Monsoon Forms’ to find the answer: What happens to the moist air when it meets mountains? (b) Explain which reading strategy (skimming or scanning) you used for each of the previous parts, and why. (c) Select the one detail from the paragraph you think would most surprise a reader, and explain your choice.
items.answer: (a) It is forced upwards, cools and forms clouds (b) Skimming for the gist/main topic; scanning for specific details such as reasons or facts. (c) Any accurate detail with a reason (e.g. a striking figure).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: It is forced upwards, cools and forms clouds [1] (b) 1 mark each strategy matched with a reason [2] (c) 1 mark detail; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Read this from an explanation text, ‘How a Monsoon Forms’: ‘As the hot air above the land rises, it creates an area of low pressure.’ What does the rising hot air create?
items.answer: An area of low pressure
items.markingKey: Retrieval: the answer is stated in the quotation (‘As the hot air above the land rises, it creates an area of low pressure.’).

items.stem: Which of these should you leave out of a summary?
options: Key information that answers the question
items.answer: Examples, descriptive detail and repetition
items.markingKey: A summary keeps only the main points.

items.stem: Rewrite this sentence in your own words: ‘The higher pressure outside pushes the eardrum inwards, which can feel uncomfortable or even painful.’
items.answer: The extra pressure in the cabin presses the eardrum in, which may hurt.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: meaning kept accurately; substantially reworded (technical terms may be kept).

items.stem: Rewrite this sentence in your own words: ‘These roots do far more than hold the trees up.’
items.answer: The roots have many other uses besides supporting the trees.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: meaning kept accurately; substantially reworded (technical terms may be kept).

items.stem: Read an information text, ‘The Waggle Dance’. ‘Honeybees cannot draw maps, but they can dance them. When a forager bee discovers a good patch of flowers, she returns to the hive and performs a “waggle dance” on the honeycomb. She runs forward in a straight line, shaking her body from side to side, then loops back round and repeats the movement. The direction of the straight run shows the direction of the food in relation to the sun. The length of the waggle tells the other bees how far away it is: the longer the waggle, the further the flight. Other workers follow the dancer closely, sensing her movements in the dark hive, and then fly off to find the flowers for themselves. The dance was first decoded by the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch, who later shared a Nobel Prize for his work.’ In no more than 40 words, summarise how the waggle dance communicates the location of food. Use your own words as far as possible.
items.answer: A returning forager waggles along a straight line: its direction gives the food’s direction relative to the sun and its length gives the distance. Nearby bees sense the movements and fly out to the flowers.
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark per valid point, up to 2: the bee runs in a straight line while waggling; the direction of the run shows the direction of the food relative to the sun; the length of the waggle shows the distance; other bees follow closely and sense the movements; they then fly to the flowers themselves. Credit concise own-words expression; no credit for copied lists or examples.

items.stem: Read this paragraph, ‘Sleep and Teenagers’: ‘Teenagers need between eight and ten hours of sleep a night, yet many get far less. During puberty, the body clock shifts, so teenagers naturally feel sleepy later in the evening. Early school starts and late-night screen use make the problem worse, because the blue light from phones delays the release of melatonin, the hormone that makes us sleepy. Lack of sleep can affect memory, mood and concentration.’ Write a summary of this paragraph in your own words (maximum 35 words).
items.answer: Model: Many teenagers sleep less than the eight to ten hours they need because their body clocks shift later, school starts early and screens delay melatonin, harming memory and mood.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: main idea captured; key supporting points included; own words; within the word limit; no examples or minor detail.

items.stem: Read an explanation text, ‘How a Monsoon Forms’. ‘Every summer, the land in South Asia heats up much faster than the surrounding ocean. As the hot air above the land rises, it creates an area of low pressure. Cooler, moist air from over the Indian Ocean is then drawn inland to replace it. This sea air carries enormous quantities of water vapour. When it meets mountains such as the Western Ghats or the Himalayas, it is forced upwards, cools and condenses into thick clouds. As a result, heavy rain falls, sometimes for weeks at a time. In winter the process reverses: the land cools more quickly than the sea, so dry winds blow from the land towards the ocean. Farmers depend on the summer monsoon, because in much of the region it brings most of the year’s rain in just a few months.’ In no more than 60 words, summarise the stages by which summer monsoon rain is formed. Use your own words as far as possible.
items.answer: In summer the land warms faster than the sea, so rising air leaves low pressure that draws moist ocean air inland. Mountains force this air upwards, where it cools and condenses into clouds that release heavy rain.
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark per valid point, up to 4: land heats faster than the sea; hot air rises, creating low pressure; moist sea air is drawn inland; air is forced up by mountains; it cools and condenses into clouds; heavy rain falls. Credit concise own-words expression; no credit for copied lists or examples.

She runs forward in a straight line, shaking her body from side to side, then loops back round and repeats the movement. The direction of the straight run shows the direction of the food in relation to the sun. The length of the waggle tells the other bees how far away it is: the longer the waggle, the further the flight. Other workers follow the dancer closely, sensing her movements in the dark hive, and then fly off to find the flowers for themselves. items.stem: Read an explanation text, ‘How a Solar Still Works’. ‘A solar still is a simple device that uses the sun’s heat to turn salty or dirty water into clean drinking water. First, a shallow basin is filled with the untreated water and covered with a sloping sheet of clear plastic or glass. Sunlight passes through the cover and warms the water, causing some of it to evaporate. The water vapour leaves salt, mud and most germs behind. When the vapour touches the cooler underside of the cover, it condenses into droplets. Because the cover slopes, these droplets run down into a collecting channel and then into a container. A small still might produce only a few litres a day, but it needs no fuel, no electricity and very little maintenance, which makes it valuable in remote, sunny places.’ Write a summary of how a solar still produces clean water for a younger student who has never studied this topic. Write one paragraph of about 80–100 words in your own words, using clear connectives to show the order or the causes.
items.answer: Model summary: Untreated water in a covered basin is warmed by sunlight and evaporates, leaving salt and dirt behind. The vapour condenses on the cool sloping cover and the droplets run down into a container.

Indicative content: untreated water is put in a covered basin; sunlight warms the water so it evaporates; impurities are left behind; vapour condenses on the cooler cover; droplets run down the slope into a container. items.stem: Rewrite this sentence in your own words: ‘it needs no fuel, no electricity and very little maintenance’
items.answer: it runs without power and hardly ever needs repairs.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: meaning kept accurately; substantially reworded (technical terms may be kept).

items.stem: What is a cohesive device?
options: A full stop at the end of a sentence
A word that describes a noun
A word or phrase that links ideas across sentences and paragraphs
items.answer: A word or phrase that links ideas across sentences and paragraphs
items.markingKey: E.g. connectives (therefore), pronouns referring back (this process), and repetition of key nouns.

items.stem: A student completed this sentence with ‘however’: ‘Many animals hibernate in winter. Bears, ____, may sleep for several months.’ Explain why ‘for example’ would be a better choice.
items.answer: ‘for example’ shows giving an example, which is the relationship between the ideas; ‘however’ signals a different relationship and confuses the logic.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: identifies the relationship (giving an example); explains why ‘however’ is wrong; credit for a clear comment on the reader’s understanding.

items.stem: A student completed this sentence with ‘However’: ‘The sun heats the water in the lake. ____, some of it evaporates.’ Explain why ‘As a result’ would be a better choice.
items.answer: ‘As a result’ shows cause and effect, which is the relationship between the ideas; ‘However’ signals a different relationship and confuses the logic.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: identifies the relationship (cause and effect); explains why ‘However’ is wrong; credit for a clear comment on the reader’s understanding.

items.stem: Here is a student’s draft explanation: ‘Lava comes out. Pressure builds up. Magma rises under the ground. The volcano erupts.’ Rewrite this explanation in the correct order and join the ideas with cohesive devices.
items.answer: Deep underground, magma rises towards the surface. As it gathers, pressure builds up in the magma chamber. Eventually the pressure becomes too great and the volcano erupts, so lava flows out.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: Award for: sequence; causal links (as, so, eventually); technical words kept accurately. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.stem: Here is a student’s draft explanation: ‘When water gets really hot it turns into steam and goes up, then it hits something cold and turns back into water again.’ Improve this explanation by using technical vocabulary and a formal, impersonal style.
items.answer: When water is heated to its boiling point, it evaporates and becomes water vapour. When the vapour meets a cold surface, it condenses back into liquid water.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: Award for: evaporates/condenses/boiling point/vapour; passive or impersonal style; clear cause and effect. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.stem: Write an explanation of why the moon appears to change shape for a younger student. Include a short introduction, steps in order and a concluding sentence. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model structure: simple question title; short definition; three or four steps with ‘first’, ‘then’, ‘as a result’; technical words explained in brackets. Key content: the moon reflects sunlight; half is always lit; as it orbits the Earth we see different amounts of the lit half; phases from new moon to full moon over about a month.

items.stem: Which tense is usually used in an information text about how something works?
options: A mixture of tenses chosen at random
items.answer: The present tense
items.markingKey: General truths and processes are written in the present (‘The heart pumps…’).

items.stem: A student is asked to find three reasons why mangroves are important. Explain how they should select information from the leaflet.
items.answer: Scan for key words such as ‘protect’, ‘shelter’ and ‘store’; select only the relevant points; ignore descriptive detail such as the spider simile.

items.stem: Read this paragraph from an information text, ‘Camels in the Desert’: ‘Camels are superbly adapted to desert life. Their wide, padded feet spread their weight so they do not sink into soft sand. Long eyelashes and nostrils that can close keep out blowing dust. Contrary to popular belief, their humps store fat, not water; the fat can be broken down for energy when food is scarce. A thirsty camel can drink over 100 litres of water in a few minutes.’ List three ways in which camels are adapted to the desert.
items.answer: Wide padded feet stop them sinking in sand; long eyelashes and closable nostrils keep out dust; humps store fat for energy; they can drink large amounts quickly.
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark per valid point, up to 2: padded feet spread weight; eyelashes/nostrils keep out dust; humps store fat for energy; drink a lot quickly.

items.stem: Read this paragraph, ‘Coral Reefs’: ‘Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they support around a quarter of all marine species. Reefs are built by tiny animals called polyps, which live in partnership with algae. The algae provide food and colour; in return, the coral provides shelter. When the water becomes too warm, the coral expels the algae and turns white, a process called bleaching. Bleached coral can recover, but it may die if the heat lasts.’ Write a summary of this paragraph in your own words (maximum 25 words).
items.answer: Model: Coral reefs, built by polyps living with algae, support a quarter of sea species; when water overheats, coral expels the algae and bleaches, and may die.

items.stem: A student completed this sentence with ‘For instance’: ‘First, the beans are picked and dried. ____, they are roasted at a high temperature.’ Explain why ‘Next’ would be a better choice.
items.answer: ‘Next’ shows sequence, which is the relationship between the ideas; ‘For instance’ signals a different relationship and confuses the logic.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: identifies the relationship (sequence); explains why ‘For instance’ is wrong; credit for a clear comment on the reader’s understanding.

items.stem: Improve this explanation by using technical vocabulary and a formal, impersonal style. ‘When water gets really hot it turns into steam and goes up, then it hits something cold and turns back into water again.’
items.answer: When water is heated to its boiling point, it evaporates and becomes water vapour. When the vapour meets a cold surface, it condenses back into liquid water.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: Award for: evaporates/condenses/boiling point/vapour; passive or impersonal style; clear cause and effect. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.stem: Here is a student’s draft explanation: ‘Plants need stuff to make food. They use light. They take in things from the air and the ground.’ Make this explanation more precise and cohesive.
items.answer: Plants make their own food by photosynthesis. Using light energy, they combine carbon dioxide from the air with water absorbed by their roots to produce glucose and oxygen.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: Award for: technical vocabulary (photosynthesis, carbon dioxide, glucose); precise nouns replacing ‘stuff’/‘things’; cohesive structure. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.stem: Which connective is most typical of an explanation text?
items.answer: therefore
items.markingKey: Explanations link causes and effects (therefore, because, as a result).

items.stem: Explain why a writer of an explanation text would use a technical vocabulary, as in: ‘It is connected to the back of the throat by a narrow passage known as the Eustachian tube.’
items.answer: Technical vocabulary: ‘Eustachian tube’ is the precise scientific name.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for identifying technical vocabulary; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: ‘Eustachian tube’ is the precise scientific name.

items.stem: Identify one feature of explanation writing in this sentence and explain its purpose: ‘It is connected to the back of the throat by a narrow passage known as the Eustachian tube.’
items.answer: Technical vocabulary: ‘Eustachian tube’ is the precise scientific name.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for the feature (technical vocabulary); 1 for the example; remaining mark(s) for its purpose for the reader.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Read this from an explanation text, ‘Why Do Your Ears Pop?’: ‘Swallowing or yawning opens the Eustachian tube briefly’ According to the text, what can open the Eustachian tube? (b) Read this from an explanation text, ‘How a Monsoon Forms’: ‘As the hot air above the land rises, it creates an area of low pressure.’ What does the rising hot air create?
items.answer: (a) Swallowing or yawning (b) An area of low pressure
items.markingKey: (a) Retrieval: the answer is stated in the quotation (‘Swallowing or yawning opens the Eustachian tube briefly’). (b) Retrieval: the answer is stated in the quotation (‘As the hot air above the land rises, it creates an area of low pressure.’).

items.stem: Why should you use the key words in a question to guide your scanning?
items.answer: The key words tell you what information to look for, so you can find the relevant part of the text quickly and avoid irrelevant details.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: identifies what to look for; efficiency/relevance.

items.stem: Read this part of an explanation text, ‘How a Monsoon Forms’: ‘Cooler, moist air from over the Indian Ocean is then drawn inland to replace it. This sea air carries enormous quantities of water vapour. In winter the process reverses: the land cools more quickly than the sea, so dry winds blow from the land towards the ocean.’ State two differences between the summer and winter monsoon winds. Use your own words where possible.
items.answer: Summer winds are moist and blow from the sea to the land; winter winds are dry and blow from the land to the sea.
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark per valid point, up to 2: direction of wind; moist versus dry; land heats in summer / cools in winter. Do not credit copied irrelevant detail.

items.stem: Read an explanation text, ‘How a Monsoon Forms’. ‘Every summer, the land in South Asia heats up much faster than the surrounding ocean. As the hot air above the land rises, it creates an area of low pressure. Cooler, moist air from over the Indian Ocean is then drawn inland to replace it. This sea air carries enormous quantities of water vapour. When it meets mountains such as the Western Ghats or the Himalayas, it is forced upwards, cools and condenses into thick clouds. As a result, heavy rain falls, sometimes for weeks at a time. In winter the process reverses: the land cools more quickly than the sea, so dry winds blow from the land towards the ocean. Farmers depend on the summer monsoon, because in much of the region it brings most of the year’s rain in just a few months.’ How does the writer make the process of the monsoon clear for the reader?
items.answer: Sequenced explanation from cause to effect; causal connectives (As a result, so, because); technical vocabulary (low pressure, condenses); present tense; contrast of summer and winter; final sentence on importance to farmers.
items.markingKey: Level-marked: top band (3–4) perceptive analysis with precise references; middle (2) clear explanation of some effects; lower (1) mainly retelling. [4]

items.stem: Read the paragraph. ‘Cities are often several degrees warmer than the countryside around them, an effect known as the urban heat island. Dark roads and roofs absorb sunlight during the day and release the heat slowly at night. Cars, air conditioners and factories add extra heat. There are also fewer trees and plants to provide shade and cool the air. Planting trees and painting roofs white are two ways to reduce the effect.’ (a) Scan an information text, ‘The Waggle Dance’ to find the answer: What does a longer waggle tell the other bees? (b) Explain which reading strategy (skimming or scanning) you used for each of the previous parts, and why. (c) Select the one detail from the paragraph you think would most surprise a reader, and explain your choice.
items.answer: (a) That the food is further away (b) Skimming for the gist/main topic; scanning for specific details such as reasons or facts. (c) Any accurate detail with a reason (e.g. a striking figure).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: That the food is further away [1] (b) 1 mark each strategy matched with a reason [2] (c) 1 mark detail; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Rewrite this sentence in your own words: ‘Mangrove forests store large amounts of carbon in their soil, helping to slow climate change.’
items.answer: The ground under mangroves holds a lot of carbon, which reduces global warming.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: meaning kept accurately; substantially reworded (technical terms may be kept).

items.stem: Rewrite this sentence in your own words: ‘much of it cleared for shrimp farms and coastal building’
items.answer: many mangroves were cut down to make way for prawn farming and construction on the coast.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: meaning kept accurately; substantially reworded (technical terms may be kept).

items.stem: Read this paragraph, ‘Clever Octopuses’: ‘Octopuses are among the most intelligent invertebrates. They can solve puzzles, open jars to reach food and even escape from aquarium tanks. An octopus has about 500 million nerve cells, and around two-thirds of them are in its arms rather than its brain, so each arm can explore and react partly on its own. Octopuses can also change the colour and texture of their skin in a fraction of a second to hide from predators.’ Summarise the main point of this paragraph in one sentence of no more than 25 words.
items.answer: Model: Octopuses are highly intelligent invertebrates that solve problems and escape tanks, have most of their nerve cells in their arms and can instantly camouflage themselves.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: main idea captured; key supporting points included; own words; within the word limit; no examples or minor detail.

items.stem: Read an explanation text, ‘How a Monsoon Forms’. ‘Every summer, the land in South Asia heats up much faster than the surrounding ocean. As the hot air above the land rises, it creates an area of low pressure. Cooler, moist air from over the Indian Ocean is then drawn inland to replace it. This sea air carries enormous quantities of water vapour. When it meets mountains such as the Western Ghats or the Himalayas, it is forced upwards, cools and condenses into thick clouds. As a result, heavy rain falls, sometimes for weeks at a time. In winter the process reverses: the land cools more quickly than the sea, so dry winds blow from the land towards the ocean. Farmers depend on the summer monsoon, because in much of the region it brings most of the year’s rain in just a few months.’ Write a summary of the stages by which summer monsoon rain is formed for a younger student who has never studied this topic. Write one paragraph of about 80–100 words in your own words, using clear connectives to show the order or the causes.
items.answer: Model summary: In summer the land warms faster than the sea, so rising air leaves low pressure that draws moist ocean air inland. Mountains force this air upwards, where it cools and condenses into clouds that release heavy rain.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 6 marks, Style and accuracy 4 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–6): all or nearly all relevant points identified; expressed concisely in own words; well organised and within the word limit; middle band (3–4): most relevant points; mostly own words; some repetition or unnecessary detail; lower band (1–2): few relevant points; much copying or irrelevant detail; may exceed the limit. Style and accuracy – top band (3–4): precise, often ambitious vocabulary chosen for effect; a wide range of sentence structures used deliberately; register consistently suited to audience and purpose; spelling, punctuation and grammar almost always accurate; middle band (2): generally appropriate vocabulary with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly suitable; occasional errors that do not obscure meaning; lower band (1): simple or repetitive vocabulary; limited sentence variety; register may slip; frequent errors in spelling, punctuation or grammar that sometimes obscure meaning. Indicative content: land heats faster than the sea; hot air rises, creating low pressure; moist sea air is drawn inland; air is forced up by mountains; it cools and condenses into clouds; heavy rain falls. Language should suit a younger reader (simple sentences, technical words explained).

items.stem: Rewrite this explanation in the correct order and join the ideas with cohesive devices. ‘Lava comes out. Pressure builds up. Magma rises under the ground. The volcano erupts.’
items.answer: Deep underground, magma rises towards the surface. As it gathers, pressure builds up in the magma chamber. Eventually the pressure becomes too great and the volcano erupts, so lava flows out.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: Award for: sequence; causal links (as, so, eventually); technical words kept accurately. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.
